JUDGMENT:
1.
The present is a complaint filed under section 16 of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 (PFA Act), alleging that the accused persons have violated the provisions of the PFA Act and Rules.

The accused no. 1 (since expired) is stated to be the vendor-cum-proprietor of M/s. Shri Govind Delhi Administration / Food Inspector vs A-1) Sh. Bharat Bhushan on 15 November, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/127928574/
1 Trading Company, from where the food article, that is, 'Vansapati' was lifted for sampling.

entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Accused no. 2 (since discharged) is stated to be the supplier and manufacturing company, of which accused no. 3 is the nominee.

2. As per the complaint, on 25.07.2002, the food officials consisting of Food Inspectors (FI) N. N.
Sharma and Virendra Singh under the supervision of Local Health Authority (LHA)/SDM Sh. V.
Valte reached along with their staff at the premises of M/s. Shri Govind Trading Company, at B-6,
Shraddhanand Market, Delhi-110006, where the accused no. 1 was found conducting the business of various food articles, which were lying stored/exposed for sale for human consumption.
The FI disclosed his identity and expressed his intention to purchase a sample of Vanaspati from the vendor as lying in sealed polythene pouches of 1 litre each, to which he agreed.
A sample of three such pouches was then lifted as per procedure prescribed under the PFA Act and Rules.
Each sample was separately packed, fastened, marked and sealed and necessary documents were prepared at the spot, including the Notice as per Form-VI, panchnama, etc.
The price of sample was paid to the vendor.
Thereafter, one counterpart of the sample was sent to the Public Analyst (PA) in intact condition and the other two counterparts were deposited with SDM/LHA.
Vide report dated 28.08.2002, the PA found the sample to be not conforming to the standards because it gave negative baudoiun test for presence of sesame oil.
Upon receipt of report, the SDM/LHA ordered investigation which was carried out by FI.
It was revealed that the accused no. 1 vendor had purchased the commodity from accused no. 2 company, of which accused no. 3 was the nominee.
After completion of investigation, sanction under section 20 of the PFA Act was obtained from the Director PFA.
The complaint was then filed in the court on 29.01.2003 alleging violation of section 2(ia)(a) and (m) of PFA Act as punishable section 7/16(1)(a) of PFA Act.
3. As the complaint was filed in writing by a public servant, recording of pre-summoning evidence was dispensed with and the accused persons were summoned vide order dated 29.01.2003.

The accused persons appeared and filed an application under section 13(2) of PFA Act thereby exercising the right to get the second counterpart of the sample to be analysed from Central Food Laboratory (CFL).
The application was allowed and a counterpart was sent for analysis to CFL.

The CFL examined the sample and its Director gave Certificate dated 31.03.2003, opining the sample to be not conforming to the PFA Rues due to presence of free fatty acids and melting point more than the prescribed maximum limits.
4. At this stage, it is pertinent to note that an application had been moved on behalf of the accused no. 2 company for dropping of the proceedings.
This application was allowed vide order dated 11.02.2004 and the proceedings were stopped against the accused no. 2 company.

Despite that,
strangely, the accused no. 3 continued to appear and represent the accused no. 2 company.
He never pointed out that the proceedings against the said accused no. 2 company already stood dropped.
For that matter, even charge was framed against all the accused persons (including accused no. 2 company) on 05.10.2005.

The matter was at the stage of PE when the court amended the charge on 27.03.2010, but again, even the amended charge (notice) was framed against all the accused persons (including accused no. 2 company the proceedings against which already stood dropped).

sentences.text: Be that as it may, after dropping the proceedings against accused no. 2 on 11.02.2004, the matter was listed for further proceedings against accused no. 1 and 3.
Apparently, the matter was summons triable in nature being violation of section 2(ia)(a) and (m) of PFA Act as punishable under section 7/16(ia)(a) of the PFA Act.

But instead of framing a notice under section 251 CrPC, two witnesses were examined on 15.02.2005 purportedly under pre-charge stage, despite the fact that there was no order of the court to summon any witness or to list the matter for PE.
6.
The complainant examined PW-1 Sh. V. Valte (SDM/LHA) and PW-2 FI N. N. Sharma in such pre-charge stage.

Based on their deposition, vide order dated 05.10.2005, charge was framed against all the accused persons for commission of the offence punishable under section 7/16(1)(a)
PFA Act, being violation of section 2(ia)(a) and (m) of PFA Act, to which they pleaded not guilty and claimed trial.

Subsequently, the witnesses already examined in pre-charge stage were recalled for further cross examination in post charge stage and additionally, the complainant examined PW-3 FI Virender Singh and PW-4 FI Arun Kumar in post charge evidence.

It is also to be noted that in the meanwhile, on 27.03.2010, the charge was amended by the court and such amended charge was framed against all the accused persons, to which they pleaded not guilty and claimed trial.
They also chose not to recall any witness already examined for further cross-examination post such amendment in the charge.
7. PW-1, PW-2 and PW-3 were part of the team that had visited the spot for sample proceedings.

All these witnesses deposed about the proceedings conducted by them on 25.07.2002 and narrated the steps undertaken by them during the sample proceedings, including disclosing their identity,
expressing intention to purchase sample for analysis, lifting the sample of 3 polythene pouches of 1 litre each of vanaspati, dividing it in three parts and putting in separate jars, fastening, sealing,
marking the sample jars, and obtaining signatures of vendor and witnesses.

They also proved the necessary documents including the vendor's receipt Ex. PW- 1/A, notice Ex. PW-1/B, Invoice Ex.
PW-1/C, Notice under section 14A Ex. PW-1/D, Panchnama Ex. PW-1/E, PA Receipt Ex. PW-2/A and LHA receipt Ex. PW-1/F.

PA report Ex. PW-1/G was received and investigation was carried out by PW-2 who sent letter Ex. PW-1/H to the STO and recorded the statement of the vendor Ex.
PW-2/B.
After completion of investigation, sanction Ex. PW-1/J was taken from the Director PFA and the complaint Ex. PW-1/K was filed in the court by the subsequent FI PW-4.
A copy of PA report with intimation letter Ex. PW- 1/L was sent to the accused persons vide postal receipt Ex. PW-1/M.
These witnesses were duly cross-examined by Ld. Defence Counsel
wherein they denied that the sampling method was not proper or that the accused persons had been falsely implicated or that representative samples were not taken.
8. Statements of the accused persons under section 313 CrPC were recorded on 15.02.2013 wherein they denied the allegations and pleaded innocence.
Accused no
. 1 claimed that he had purchased the commodity from accused no. 2 against a proper bill and had sold it in same condition as was purchased.
Accused no. 2 and 3 on the other hand, disputed the PA and CFL reports on the ground of variation between the two.
They however did not lead evidence in defence.

9. It is in these circumstances, Ld. SPP for the complainant has argued that the complainant has been able to establish its case against the accused no. 2 and 3 beyond reasonable doubt (accused no.

3 1 having already expired), on the ground that the accused persons have not been able to rebut the findings in the CFL report dated 31.03.2003 which as per section 13(3) of PFA Act is final and conclusive.

entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: It is submitted that all the witnesses have supported its case and no major contradiction can be seen in their testimony.

10. On the other hand, Ld. Defence Counsel has submitted that the sample proceedings were not conducted properly and that there are various contradictions and missing links in the testimony of witnesses.

Ld. Counsel has strongly contended that there is variation in the reports as given by PA and CFL, which leads to conclusion that the two samples were not representative and therefore,
conviction cannot be based solely on the basis of the CFL report.
He has relied upon the various judgements in his support.
He has now argued that when the accused no. 2 company itself has been discharged, its nominee accused no. 3 could be prosecuted under vicarious liability.
11. I have heard the arguments advanced by Ld. SPP for the complainant and Ld. Defence Counsel for the accused persons and have carefully perused the material available on record.
12. In a criminal case, the burden is only on the prosecution to prove its case against the accused beyond reasonable doubt by leading positive evidence.
This burden cannot be shifted to the accused and it has to be necessary discharged by the prosecution itself.

13. It is to be seen that the complaint was filed against accused no. 2 company as well as its nominee accused no. 3 on the ground that he was in charge of and responsible to the company for its business affairs, in terms of section 17 of PFA Act.

At the same time, it is seen that the proceedings against the said accused no. 2 company have already been dropped vide order dated 11.02.2004 relying upon the judgement titled as Assistant Commissioner, Assessment-II, Banglore v. M/s Velliappa Textiles Limited [2003 RCR (Criminal) 695 SC].

entities.text: Assistant Commissioner, Assessment-II, Banglore v. M/s Velliappa Textiles Limited [2003 RCR (Criminal) 695 SC]
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Needless to say, the said order has attained finality as it has never been challenged by the prosecution / complainant.

Irrespective of the fact that the court continued to mark its presence through accused no. 3 at subsequent proceedings, and also the said company continued to participate at the trial, cross-examine the witness and even record statement through its AR, the position is, that the order dated 11.02.2004 has never been nullified or modified.
The said order exists and remains in full force even today.
Even if the company continued to participate at the trial despite this order, the effect of the said order cannot be left redundant by now proceeding against the company.

This court has no power to recall its orders and therefore, the proceedings against the accused no. 2 company have to be considered as dropped in terms of order dated 11.02.2004.
14.

The question at this stage would therefore be whether the present complaint can proceed and accused no. 3 could be convicted in the capacity of nominee of company which has already been discharged by the court and such order having attained finality.
15. Earlier, there were divergent views of various Hon'ble Courts as to if a criminal complaint is maintainable against the director of a company without implicating the company as an accused.

However, the law has been now settled by the authoritative judgement of the Hon'ble Supreme Court of India titled as Aneeta Hada v. Godfather Travels and Travels Pvt. Ltd. [(2012) 5 SCC 661].

sentences.text: In the said precedent, which pertains to the interpretation of section 141 of the Negotiable Instruments Act (NI Act), Hon'ble Supreme Court of India has held that commission of offence by the company is an express condition precedent to attract the vicarious liability of other persons and therefore, it is absolutely clear that only when a company can be prosecuted that the persons mentioned in other categories could be held vicariously liable for the offence committed by the company.

The Hon'ble Supreme Court of India overruled the previous judgements titled as Sheoratan Agarwal v. State of Madhya Pradash [(1984) 4 SCC 352] and Anil Hada v. Indian Acrylic Ltd. [(2000) 1 SCC 1] and reiterated the law as laid down in State of Madras v. C.V. Parekh [(1970) 3 SCC 491].

entities.text: Sheoratan Agarwal v. State of Madhya Pradash [(1984) 4 SCC 352]
entities.label: PRECEDENT

entities.text: Anil Hada v. Indian Acrylic Ltd. [(2000) 1 SCC 1]
entities.label: PRECEDENT

entities.text: State of Madras v. C.V. Parekh [(1970) 3 SCC 491]
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Upon going through the law so laid down, it is clear that the prime liability is on the company and it is only when the court comes to conclusion that an offence has been committed by a company that it can proceed to attribute vicarious liability to other persons who are proved to be in charge of or responsible to the company for its affairs.

In the absence of the company as an accused,
the other persons including directors / shareholders / employees cannot be prosecuted independently.

16. The language of section 17 of PFA Act is pari materia to section 141 of NI Act, with respect to the role and responsibility of the persons who can be arrayed as an accused in addition to the company itself.

Like section 141 NI Act, even section 17 of PFA Act provides that in addition to the company,
any person who was in charge of or responsible to the company for its affairs can also be implicated as an accused.
If a nominee has been appointed by a company, he shall be deemed to be so responsible or in charge.

17. On the touchstone of the above discussed proportions of law, the court has to see if the accused no. 3 herein can be held liable for the offence allegedly committed by the accused no. 2 company that has already been discharged by the court.
18. Since the company itself has already been discharged and such order has already attained finality, no vicarious liability can be fastened on its nominee.

It would be a very anomolous situation to say that the company on which the principal liability would be there has already been discharged but its nominee on whom only a secondary or vicarious liability is attributable has been held guilty.
As clarified in the above mentioned precedents, no conviction of any director can be maintained in the absence of conviction of the company itself.
But when no such liability can be fastened to the company which has already been discharged by the court, no vicarious liability can be attributed even to its director or nominee.
It is not a case where a company could not be implicated on account of some technical defect or some legal incapacity.
Rather the company has been discharged by a judicial order which has attained finality and never challenged.

In view of this position, no criminal liability can be fastened on accused no. 3.
19.
Even on merits, it is to be understood that the charge/notice framed against the accused persons is for violation of section 2(ia)(a) and (m) of the PFA Act on the basis of CFL report.

Under section 2(ia)(a) of PFA Act, the prosecution has to establish that the purchaser had demanded a food article of a specific nature, substance or quality and the article sold was, to his prejudice, either not of the nature, substance or quality demanded, or was not of the nature, substance or quality which it purported or represented to be.

Section 2(ia)(m) of PFA Act deals with situation where the quality or Delhi Administration / Food Inspector vs A-1) Sh. Bharat Bhushan on 15 November, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/127928574/
5 purity of an article falls below the prescribed standard or its constituents are present in quantities not within the prescribed limits of variability.
20.

sentences.text: In the case at hand, it is an admitted position, as is clear from the report of CFL that the food article fell under Item A.19 of Appendix-B of the PFA Rules.
Specific standards have been prescribed for this food product under this provision.
21. As per section 13(3) of the PFA Act, the certificate issued by the Director of CFL shall supersede the report of the PA.
As per proviso to section 13(5) of the Act, such certificate shall be final and conclusive evidence for the facts stated therein.
Thus, as far as the findings of the CFL are concerned, the same are final and conclusive and no evidence can be given to disprove the same.

22. In Calcutta Municipal Corporation v. Pawan Kumar Saraf [AIR 1999 SC 738], it has been authoritatively laid down that the legal impact of a certificate of the Director of CFL is three fold: (a)
it annuls or replaces the report of the PA, (b) it gains finality regarding the quality and standard of the food article involved in the case and (c) it becomes irrefutable so far as the facts stated therein are concerned.
23.

entities.text: Calcutta Municipal Corporation v. Pawan Kumar Saraf [AIR 1999 SC 738]
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: In Subhash Chander v. State, Delhi Administration [1983(4) DRJ 100], it was observed by Hon'ble High Court of Delhi that "It has repeatedly been held by the supreme court that the certificate of the Director supersedes the report of the public analyst and is to be treated as conclusive evidence of its contents.

entities.text: Subhash Chander v. State, Delhi Administration [1983(4) DRJ 100]
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: The Director is a greater expert and therefore the statute says that his certificate shall be accepted by the court as conclusive evidence.
For all purposes the report of the public analyst is replaced by the certificate of the Director....
Superseded is a strong word.
It means obliterate, set aside, annul, replace, make void, inefficacious or useless, repeal.
The Director's cetificate supersedes the report given by the public analyst.
Once superseded it does not survive for any purpose.
It will be anamolous to hold that for some purpose it survives and for other purposes it is superseded."
24. Since the report of CFL is final and conclusive and the same supersedes the report of PA, only this report has to be considered and the report of PA has to be ignored.
It would be seen that the CFL report has negated the results of PA on the major counts.
The Baudoin Test which was found negative by the PA, was found positive by the CFL and as per the standards.
On the contrary, the melting point found by the PA at 41 degree (as per standards) was found to be 45.5 degrees by the CFL (beyond range).

The free fatty acid content found by the PA to be 0.35% was found by the CFL to be 0.43%.
25.

In this regard, the defence strongly relies upon the judgement titled as Kanshi Nath v. State [2005(2) FAC 219], informing that the said ruling has been constantly followed by the Hon'ble High Court of Delhi in State v. Ramesh Chand [2010 (2) JCC 1250], Food Inspector v. sentences.text: It is submitted that comparison of the two reports would show that there are substantive variations which would show that the sample was not representative.

26. The Hon'ble High Court of Delhi in Kashi Nath's case (supra), was dealing with a situation where there were certain variations in the reports of PA and CFL while analysing a sample of 'dhania powder'.

Hon'ble Court considered the ratio in MCD v. Bishan Sarup [ILR 1970 (1) Delhi 518] and held that it would still be open for the accused to establish that the sample tested was not a representative one, and if the variation in the two reports is substantial enough, then the PA report can certainly be looked into to establish this variation.
27.
Though the CFL report is final and conclusive as to the results therein, yet it can still be looked into to ascertain if the samples were representative or not.

If the accused is able to show that the samples were not representative or otherwise that the food article might have undergone a change by the time it reached CFL which was beyond his control, he would get benefit on that count.
28. In the case at hand, the differences between the two reports would show substantive variations in the two reports.
There is vast difference in the Baudouin Test result and the Melting points by the two analysts.
Thus, the incriminating matter on the basis of which prosecution was launched, stood negated by CFL.
29. As far as the ground on which CFL failed the sample is concerned, it is important to understand that vanaspati as a food article is prone to natural variations.
If quality or purity of such an article falls below the prescribed standards solely due to natural causes and beyond the control of human agency, then such article would not be termed as adulterated.
If the two reports are so considered, it would lead to inference that the two samples were not representative or of same lot or quality.
The melting point would not have changed with the passage of time.
Similarly, sesame oil would not have developed in the food article with the passage of time.

And when the samples are at variance on these two major parameters, it would not be safe to convict a person solely on the basis of increased fatty acid content, which does changes with the passage of time.
The CFL had examined the sample from 24.03.2003 to 31.03.2003.
Thus, it was so analysed after about 08 months when it was lifted from the possession of the accused no. 1.
The nature of vanaspati as a food product is such that some changes are bound to happen if sample is kept for a long period.

The effect of presence of moisture,
temperature, external environment, internal heat etc. cannot be ignored on such article, particularly when no preservative as such was used in the sample.
Such changes would be natural changes beyond human control.

Content of Free Fatty Acids increases in sample of vanaspati with the passage of time, particularly after its shelf life. Form-VI Ex. PW-1/B would show that the vanaspati was manufactured in June 2002 and its best before date was mentioned to be six months.
Thus, if free fatty acid content goes beyond limit after December 2002, that might be a natural cause as well.
The sample was analysed by the CFL after such best before date and possibility of natural changes cannot be ruled out as far as free fatty acid content is considered.

Reliance can be placed on the judgements titled as National Diary Development Board v. State of Haryana [1997(I) PFA Cases 95]
and Nebh Raj v. State [Crl. Appeal No. 113/1975, Supreme Court of India, dated 24.10.1980].

sentences.text: persons
can be convicted, particularly in view of such substantive variations in the two reports.
The only conclusion would be that either the sample was not truly representative or otherwise it underwent a natural change during the intervening period which was beyond human control.
In any case, the accused persons would get a benefit of doubt.
30. Thus, the matter would not be covered under section 2(ia)(a) of PFA Act.

There is no evidence to show that any particular nature, quality or substance of vanaspati was demanded by the FI which was not supplied to him to his prejudice, or that it was not of nature, quality or substance represented or purported to be so as to bring the case within section 2(ia)
(a) of PFA Act.
As far as section 2(ia)(m) is concerned, the accused no. 3 is entitled to be given benefit of doubt considering the time gap, natural variations and variations in two reports.

The evidence on record is not sufficient to conclude that the sample in question was 'adulterated' within the meaning of section 2(ia) of PFA Act and thus, no case would be made out against the accused no.
3 for commission of offences punishable under section 7/16 of the PFA Act.
31.
Having said so, the accused no. 3 is acquitted of the charges (accused no. 1 has already expired and proceedings against accused no. 2 have already been dropped).

However, his bail bonds shall remain in force for the next six months in terms of section 437-A, CrPC.
32.
File be consigned to record room.

opennyai_summary.ANALYSIS:
12. In a criminal case, the burden is only on the prosecution to prove its case against the accused beyond reasonable doubt by leading positive evidence.
13. It is to be seen that the complaint was filed against accused no. 2 company as well as its nominee accused no. 3 on the ground that he was in charge of and responsible to the company for its business affairs, in terms of section 17 of PFA Act.
At the same time, it is seen that the proceedings against the said accused no. 2 company have already been dropped vide order dated 11.02.2004 relying upon the judgement titled as Assistant Commissioner, Assessment-II, Banglore v. M/s Velliappa Textiles Limited [2003 RCR (Criminal) 695 SC].
The Hon'ble Supreme Court of India overruled the previous judgements titled as Sheoratan Agarwal v. State of Madhya Pradash [(1984) 4 SCC 352] and Anil Hada v. Indian Acrylic Ltd. [(2000) 1 SCC 1] and reiterated the law as laid down in State of Madras v. C.V. Parekh [(1970) 3 SCC 491].
Upon going through the law so laid down, it is clear that the prime liability is on the company and it is only when the court comes to conclusion that an offence has been committed by a company that it can proceed to attribute vicarious liability to other persons who are proved to be in charge of or responsible to the company for its affairs.
In the absence of the company as an accused,
the other persons including directors / shareholders / employees cannot be prosecuted independently.
16. The language of section 17 of PFA Act is pari materia to section 141 of NI Act, with respect to the role and responsibility of the persons who can be arrayed as an accused in addition to the company itself.
If a nominee has been appointed by a company, he shall be deemed to be so responsible or in charge.
17. On the touchstone of the above discussed proportions of law, the court has to see if the accused no. 3 herein can be held liable for the offence allegedly committed by the accused no. 2 company that has already been discharged by the court.
18. Since the company itself has already been discharged and such order has already attained finality, no vicarious liability can be fastened on its nominee.
But when no such liability can be fastened to the company which has already been discharged by the court, no vicarious liability can be attributed even to its director or nominee.
It is not a case where a company could not be implicated on account of some technical defect or some legal incapacity.
Rather the company has been discharged by a judicial order which has attained finality and never challenged.
Even on merits, it is to be understood that the charge/notice framed against the accused persons is for violation of section 2(ia)(a) and (m) of the PFA Act on the basis of CFL report.
22. In Calcutta Municipal Corporation v. Pawan Kumar Saraf [AIR 1999 SC 738], it has been authoritatively laid down that the legal impact of a certificate of the Director of CFL is three fold: (a)
it annuls or replaces the report of the PA, (b) it gains finality regarding the quality and standard of the food article involved in the case and (c) it becomes irrefutable so far as the facts stated therein are concerned.
23.
Thus, if free fatty acid content goes beyond limit after December 2002, that might be a natural cause as well.
The sample was analysed by the CFL after such best before date and possibility of natural changes cannot be ruled out as far as free fatty acid content is considered.
Reliance can be placed on the judgements titled as National Diary Development Board v. State of Haryana [1997(I) PFA Cases 95]
and Nebh Raj v. State [Crl. Appeal No. 113/1975, Supreme Court of India, dated 24.10.1980].

There is no evidence to show that any particular nature, quality or substance of vanaspati was demanded by the FI which was not supplied to him to his prejudice, or that it was not of nature, quality or substance represented or purported to be so as to bring the case within section 2(ia)
(a) of PFA Act.
As far as section 2(ia)(m) is concerned, the accused no. 3 is entitled to be given benefit of doubt considering the time gap, natural variations and variations in two reports.
The evidence on record is not sufficient to conclude that the sample in question was 'adulterated' within the meaning of section 2(ia) of PFA Act and thus, no case would be made out against the accused no.
